---
title: "5. Alpha diversity (within-sample)"
format:
  html:
    toc: false
---

*Complement the between-sample view from [step 4](tutorial-04-pcoa.qmd) with diversity **within** each sample — alpha diversity — using the [Shannon index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversity_index#Shannon_index){target="_blank"}.*

While step 4's PCoA shows whether community *composition* differs between habitats (beta diversity — how communities differ from one another), this step asks a different, complementary question: do some habitats simply host more diverse communities *within* a single sample (alpha diversity), regardless of how that composition compares to other samples?

### Calculate Shannon diversity per sample

We reuse `counts_filt`, the cluster-aggregated matrix built in [step 4](tutorial-04-pcoa.qmd), instead of building a second large dense matrix:

```r
shannon <- vegan::diversity(counts_filt, MARGIN = 2)
```

### Plot Shannon diversity by habitat

```r
par(mar = c(7, 4, 2, 1))
boxplot(shannon ~ habitat[ix], las = 2, xlab = "",
        ylab = "Shannon diversity",
        col = habitat_cols[levels(factor(habitat[ix]))])
```

Interpretation: a habitat with a high median and narrow spread here hosts consistently diverse communities; a wide spread means diversity varies a lot from sample to sample within that habitat. This is independent of the PCoA result in step 4 — a habitat could look distinct in composition (beta diversity) while being just as diverse, more diverse, or less diverse than others within a sample (alpha diversity).
